title: Role of Class IIa HDACs HDAC4 and HDAC7 in Pathogenic Th17 Cell Development and Colitis
text:
This project aims to delineate the function roles of Hdac4 and Hdac7 in Th17 cell development and
inflammatory bowel diseases. The outcome will empower the research community to better understand the
fundamental molecular basis of Th17 cell transcriptional program and pathogenicity, and will have great
implications in human health and autoimmune diseases, particularly inflammatory bowel diseases.

title: Collaborative Union for Cancer Research, and Educational Development (CURED)
text: The BCM-TSU P20 “Collaborative Union for Cancer Research, and Educational Development (CURED)” Proposal will establish a formal collaborative alliance between BCM and TSU for cancer research, education, and community outreach. Our multipronged approach will maximize the strengths of each institution and leverage existing collaborative relationships to create a shared infrastructure between BCM and TSU that will provide an optimal environment for cancer research, education, community outreach, and opportunities for career development and pathway enhancement focused on augmenting the biomedical workforce. BCM-TSU P20 CURED will also develop sustainable research capacity and obtain preliminary data through pilot projects that will develop into independent investigator research applications and collaborative applications to the NIH/NCI and/or other Federal/Non-federal funding agencies.

title: Interdisciplinary Health Research (IHER) Center
text:
Interdisciplinary Health Equity Research Center
Public Health Relevance
Summary
Because of the diversity of their faculty and students, and places of
trust in the community, HBCUs such as Delaware State University, are
strategically poised to make important scientific contributions addressing the serious
problem of racial/ethnic health disparities. Support from the RCMI program to establish
the Interdisciplinary Health Equity Research Center at DSU will build a capacity for
biomedical, behavioral and social research targeting understanding and reducing health
disparities. The Center will support early stage investigators to reach the level of research
capability competitive for external funding and necessary to pursue discovery science
that will translate into improvements in the health status of minority individuals and
communities.

title: Strategies to predict and overcome resistance to cancer immunotherapy
text:
The discovery that there are simple ways to turn our own defense mechanisms against
cancer was revolutionary, leading to unprecedented cures of some patients with
advanced disease that had never been possible with surgery, radiation, and
chemotherapy. Unfortunately, this miraculous treatment, called immunotherapy, does
not work as often as it should, and it remains a mystery why people with the same type
of cancer will have different responses to the same treatment. The experiments being
supported by this project are intended to create a blood test to predict whether cancer
immunotherapy will work or not and also to provide a solution for patients who are not
likely to respond, by adding a second medication to their treatment, which will increase
their chances of responding to immunotherapy.

title: Arid5b regulation of pathogenic fibroblast states
text: In RA, the synovial membrane becomes profoundly infiltrated with T cells, B cells, macrophages and other inflammatory leukocytes. As a mesenchymal tissue, it also undergoes striking hyperplasia of the parenchymal synovial fibroblasts. Appreciation for the central role that the synovial fibroblasts play in the disease has grown. Recent studies using synovial biopsies reveal that fibroblast-dominant synovial infiltrates define the synovial phenotype most correlated with non-response to targeted therapies. This underscores the importance of targeting fibroblasts as treatment-inadequate responders constitute the main unmet in RA. Functionally, fibroblasts are a major inflammatory cell population in RA synovium, producing nearly all the IL-6 as well as high levels of chemokines that recruit and sustain the infiltrating leukocytes. Besides this inflammatory role, fibroblasts also dominate in driving structural damage in the joint by directly invading and degrading the cartilage and bone matrix and indirectly as the major source of RANKL that activates osteoclasts. For decades, it has been assumed that the same activated fibroblasts mediated both these inflammatory and invasive roles. However, recent evidence from mouse models suggests that different populations of fibroblasts mediate these roles independently (Croft et al Nature 2019, DOI 10.1038/s41586- 019-1263-7). We sought the identity of transcription factors that might regulate the phenotypic switch determining if activated synovial fibroblasts become inflammatory or invasive. In preliminary data, we identified ARID5B, as a transcription factor that binds demethylases and deacetylases and localizes them to the promotors of inflammatory and invasive gene loci, thus epigenetically regulating fibroblast inflammatory versus invasive programs in a reciprocal manner. Functionally, we show that CRISPR deletion of ARID5B in stimulated RA synovial fibroblasts results in higher inflammatory product production and nearly silenced invasion activity. In contrast, CRISPRa over-expression of ARID5B produces an invasive fibroblast with a markedly reduced inflammatory phenotype. Thus, we hypothesize that ARID5B is responsible for reciprocally regulating the inflammatory versus invasive fibroblast gene programs. Our analysis of scRNAseq data supports an ARID5B driven phenotype in fibroblast-enriched cell type abundance phenotype synovium (called CTAP-F) where fibroblasts with an invasive/degradative gene program are dominant. In Aim 1 we determine if the expression of Arid5b-regulated fibroblast gene programs underlie particular RA synovial subtypes and treatment non-responders. In Aim 2, we define ARID5B causal alleles and eQTLs using a novel CRISPR allele editing platform. And finally in Aim 3, we determine the effects of Arid5b deletion or overexpression in fibroblasts on inflammation and structural damage in a murine model of inflammatory arthritis. Together, these studies will define a major regulator of pathologic fibroblast effector functions relevant in fibroblast-dominated non-responder patient populations.

title: Epigenetic Regulation of KLF4 in SSc-associated lung fibrosis
text:
This project will identify epigenetic mechanisms that result in the observed downregulation of
KLF4 in scleroderma lung fibroblasts. A better understanding of these regulatory mechanisms will
allow us to design effective therapeutic strategies to restore normal KLF4 levels and ameliorate
fibrosis.

title: 3D Spatial Multi-Omics Profiling of Ovarian Cancer
text:
The proposed study seeks to use multiple state-of-the–art molecular and cellular profiling platforms to
construct a three-dimensional spatially resolved Ovarian Cancer Atlas using treatment naïve formalin fixed
paraffin embedded (FFPE) ovarian tumor tissue samples obtained from the primary ovarian site and metastatic
sites in racially diverse patients who are diagnosed with chemo-refractory or chemo-sensitive advanced high-
grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). We expect that the results will be used by academic researchers,
clinical researchers and industry partners to improve our understanding of the molecular basis of the disease
and better strategize disease management of patients. In addition, the results of this study would have the
potential leading to the development of clinical trials testing novel agents against new molecular targets.

title: Investigating fundamental signal transduction mechanisms impacted by FOXO transcription factors on NOTCH and JAK/STAT Pathways in stem cell contexts
text:
This study utilizes innovative genomics techniques to address critical barriers to understanding
FOXO transcription factor-driven developmental and cellular processes that promote stem cell
fate specification and function in the contexts of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and myoblasts.
Single cell RNA Seq will be used to determine whether FOXO transcription factors drive the
fundamental developmental NOTCH Pathway within the context of stem cells and/or in
neighboring differentiated cells. This study will also investigate the differential impacts of FOXO
factors on the JAK/STAT Pathway in stem cell settings.

title: Biofabrication Training Program
text:
Biofabrication merges materials science processing with controlled cellular behavior, with impacts on fields such
as tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, drug delivery, three-dimensional cell culture, and in vitro tissue
models. To further impact these fields and to educate a future workforce, new training programs are needed that
not only educate in quantitative fundamentals and biofabrication techniques, but also drive the intersection of
basic research and commercialization. Through our innovative training program, including a biofabrication
course, industry exposure, co-mentorship to harness the expertise of Preceptors, and a bi-weekly seminar
series, our Trainees will be poised to make a meaningful impact on society through biomedicine.

title: Molecular mechanism of regulation and activation of membrane proteins in native membrane milieu
text:
I will develop an experimental pipeline that is broadly applicable to study the molecular mechanism of regulation
and activation of membrane/membrane-associated proteins in the context of their endogenous environment, by
extracting them while retaining an annular ring of their local protein and lipid interactome (native nanodiscs).
These native nanodiscs can be used in several biophysical and biochemical analyses to understand the structural
and functional organization, spatially-enriched endogenous proteomic and lipidomic environments, and
ultimately bioactivity of target membrane proteins embedded in them. I propose to apply this pipeline and
downstream analyses to investigate (1) a small, clinically relevant GTPase that is a hallmark oncogene, and (2) a
receptor tyrosine kinase family that is critical for neuronal survival and development and plays a crucial role in
pain perception.

title: Project 3: Molecular Risk Stratification of Gastric Precancerous Lesions
text:
This project is geared towards developing better ways of detecting stomach cancer in its earliest stages when 
there is a high chance of cure. This research will lead to ways of reducing the risk of developing stomach cancer.

title: Integrating Multi-Modal Data and Biomechanics in COPD: Toward Robust and Interpretable Biomarkers for Disease Subtyping and Progression
text:
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a progressive disease affecting 300M worldwide with a
substantial economic burden. This project develops a computational method to integrate information from
imaging, genomic data, and biomechanical modeling to enhance the precision and interpretation of disease
progression and subtyping. Insights and tools developed in this project have an impact beyond COPD to other
pulmonary diseases.

title: Tumor-derived Cell-membrane Coated NanoVaccine (TCC-NV) as personalized neoantigen immunotherapy to enhance efficacy of TNBC treatments
text:
Despite the significant potential of neoantigen-based cancer vaccines to improve clinical outcomes of TNBC,
substantial challenges remain in developing fast, efficient, and cost-effective personalized neoantigen-based
immunotherapies. To address these challenges, we will engineer personalized nanovaccines distinguished by
their rapid and simplified production methods, functioning as an "on-demand" formulation platform tailored to
individual patient and tumor characteristics. By inducing robust T cell immunity, nanovaccines are designed to
target both solid tumors and microscopic metastatic lesions, improving treatment outcomes while preventing
recurrence and future metastasis.

title: Community Outreach and Engagement
text: The UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center (LCCC) has a long history of serving the state of North Carolina (NC) through clinical care, research, policy, and cancer-focused outreach and community engagement. Since receiving NCI cancer center designation in 1975 and comprehensive status in 1990, LCCC has served as the only public comprehensive cancer center in NC with patients, outreach, and research efforts in all 100 NC counties. Based on its history of conducting impactful research and delivering cancer care to patients from all 100 NC counties, LCCC defined its catchment area a decade ago as the entire state of NC. The state has the 9th largest population in the US. Notably, LCCC and its clinical venue, UNC Hospitals, have been directly responsible to the people and legislature of NC for ensuring that high quality, accessible cancer care is provided to NC residents regardless of their ability to pay; in a state without Medicaid expansion, this is an important responsibility. For decades, LCCC-supported research and outreach efforts have been committed to defining and implementing cancer practice and policies that are evidence-based and designed to address specific needs in the catchment area. These responsibilities are now coordinated by the LCCC Community Outreach and Engagement (COE) Office, whose mission it is to meaningfully engage the community in cancer research, clinical care and programmatic and policy efforts to understand and serve the population's needs. COE’s vision and objective are to develop and sustain active community partnerships to reduce the burden of cancer and eliminate cancer disparities in NC and beyond. The specific aims of the COE Office are to: (1) monitor the cancer burden and identify cancer health disparities in NC; (2) synergize institutional and community efforts to engage a variety of stakeholders in addressing the cancer burden and reducing cancer health disparities in NC; (3) coordinate and amplify cancer outreach and supportive care with a variety of stakeholder audiences; and (4) facilitate impactful cancer research in NC and beyond. The COE Office ensures that LCCC research, clinical care, and programmatic outreach efforts are timely, relevant, responsive, and infused with community perspectives, including policy makers, community providers and public health practitioners, cancer patients and caregivers, and the public at large. The impact of the work is expected to reduce cancer morbidity and mortality in NC and beyond.

title: Probing the Mechanism of HIV-1 Gag Localization to Transcription Sites
text:
AIDS remains an international health crisis, and resistance to current therapies presents an ongoing challenge
to eliminating HIV-1 infection. This research project investigates how HIV-1 Gag hijacks transcription-related
host factors to localize to transcription sites to bind viral RNA and produce infectious virus particles. Innovative
approaches will be used in this exploratory project, with the ultimate goal of identifying virus-cell interactions
that could be disrupted to interfere with the spread of HIV-1.

title: Advanced Base and Prime Editing Strategies to Correct Common ALS-causing SOD1 Mutations
text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a devastating neurodegenerative disease that leads to death within 5 years of diagnosis. This proposal seeks to develop and validate somatic gene correction strategies for common mutations in familial SOD1-ALS in vivo, using base editing and prime editing. This project will explore new methods for somatic gene correction that are broadly relevant to many genetic disorders of the CNS.

title: Mass Spectrometric Studies of Neuropeptides in Feeding
text:
The growing incidence of eating disorders and obesity, and their associated health costs have led to intensive
research efforts directed at understanding the mechanisms and signaling pathways that control and regulate
food intake. This competitive renewal grant application aims at developing innovative mass spectrometry-
based technologies and strategies in combination with physiological approaches to characterize neuropeptides
and biogenic amines involved in feeding with increased sensitivity, accuracy and throughput. The molecular
insights gained from this research promise to increase our knowledge about peptidergic signaling and
neuromodulation in the regulation of this essential physiological process, which could ultimately lead to the
development of new therapeutic strategies for obesity and eating disorders that have become a big concern of
modern societies.

title: Hybrid Biological-Abiotic Proximity Labeling Catalysts for Enhancing Spatially-Resolved Proteomics
text:
Martell project narrative (2-3 sentences)
Technologies that enable the identification of which proteins reside in specific locations inside
cells are critical for elucidating biological processes and disease states, including
neurodegeneration, pathogenic infection, and cancer. One promising strategy to achieve this goal
is proximity labeling (PL), but in order to enhance the sensitivity and specificity of proximal protein
detection, improved PL catalysts are needed. We propose that hybrid biological-abiotic PL
catalysts developed in our laboratory will enhance both sensitivity and specificity in spatially-
resolved proteomic mapping, and we are employing these catalysts in neurons to benchmark their
performance against existing methods and establish their broad utility as research tools.

title: Environmental Health Data Science Core
text: ENIRONMENTAL HEALTH DATA SCIENCE CORE ABSTRACT The Environmental Health Data Science Core (EHDSC) provides a wide range of support in biostatistics, statistical genetics and genomics, bioinformatics, machine learning/ artificial intelligence (ML/AI), and data management and sharing for investigators associated with the Center. Assistance is also available in several other specialized areas including environmental epidemiology and the geographic information sciences (GIS). In addition to study design and analysis support, Core faculty and staff advise Center investigators on principles as well as statistical and computational tools for reproducible science, including data management, large-scale research computing infrastructure, analysis pipelines, and data sharing plans. Further, Core faculty and staff provide statistical and bioinformatics training for faculty, graduate students, and fellows working on Center-related projects. Core faculty engage in mission-related methodological research motivated by questions and methodological challenges, providing freely available software to Center members and the broader environmental health community. The Core interfaces directly with the Center’s other components, including the Translational Research Support Core (TRSC), the Community Engagement Core (CEC), and the Pilot Project Program (PPP). Providing such services via a core facility allows us to build and maintain specialized resources (e.g., expertise in advanced statistical methods, statistical genetics and genomics, bioinformatics, and geographic information systems) while also drawing on the broader resources available through the Program in Environmental Statistics and the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. We are able to leverage our Center support with University resources to maximize our services to Center members.

title: Viral Vector and Regulatory Core
text: VIRAL VECTOR AND REGULATORY CORE Translation of a laboratory discovery to a clinical trial generates many management and regulatory challenges. Gene editing brings additional safety issues to the fore, such as the adverse consequences of off-target editing, that require creativity and experience to properly investigate, quantify, and mitigate as needed. The Viral Vector and Regulatory Core brings the necessary expertise and history of collaboration across U19 team members to offer two critical services to this U19: scaled production of all AAV vectors to ensure consistently high quality of these biological reagents for therapeutic testing in the projects; and practical guidance and support to help the projects navigate the regulatory path to an IND submission. Key innovations include access to a scalable manufacturing system for AAV9 available through the Translational Gene Therapy Core at UTSW, which is directed by the Viral Vector and Regulatory Core Lead Steven Gray. The continuity of AAV product quality and potency offered through the Translational Gene Therapy Core will streamline the regulatory process and avoid costly and time-consuming bridging studies. A second innovation developed by the Core team are preclinical and clinical immune-management protocols for delivery of non-self transgenes. Since any gene editing–based treatment developed through this Program is expected to be viewed as non-self by the recipient's immune system, incorporation of these strategies is likely to be critical for the preclinical and clinical success. Close engagement with the Genome Editing Core on vector design and interpretation of genome editing results, and with the Preclinical Mouse Model Core on study design to assure all assessments are aligned with IND requirements, will be thoroughly woven into the pipeline to optimize efficiency. The approach to achieve the Viral Vector and Regulatory Core's goals will leverage best practices based on the experience of the Core Lead, supporting staff and consultants that have resulted in numerous successful pre-IND and IND submissions for AAV-based therapeutics. The significance of the Core is that it will ensure that all activities in the projects and other cores meet FDA quality expectations, and will work proactively to avoid unnecessary delays or work repetition to meet those expectations. This is central to the overall aims of this U19 Program and is critical, particularly for research labs that have not gone through the translational process. The Specific Aims are: 1) To support the U19 projects by supplying AAV vectors; 2) To conduct an INTERACT meeting to understand FDA expectations for pre-clinical proof of concept data of the lead project therapeutic entity; 3) To conduct a type B pre-IND meeting and coordinate IND-enabling studies; and 4) To coordinate parties to assemble and submit an allowable IND.
